title_options: How Hard Could A T. rex Bite? 🦖
facts: Gignac & Erickson 2017, Scientific Reports 7:2012 (doi:10.1038/s41598-017-02161-w): adult T. rex bite force up to 34,522 N at the posterior teeth; tooth pressures up to 2,974 MPa; jaw muscles reconstructed using its closest living relatives (crocodylians and birds).
Erickson et al. 2012, PLoS ONE 7:e31781 (doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0031781): saltwater crocodile 16,414 N, the highest bite force measured in a living animal.
Chin et al. 1998, Nature 393:680 (doi:10.1038/31461): a king-sized theropod coprolite, most likely from T. rex, 30-50% bone fragments.
34,522 N = about 3,520 kg-force, roughly three small cars of ~1,200 kg.
description: One T. rex bite pressed down like three small cars stacked on its teeth. Here's how scientists worked it out, and the fossil poop that proves it crushed bone. #shorts #dinosaurs #TRex #Science
sources: Gignac & Erickson 2017, Scientific Reports (doi:10.1038/s41598-017-02161-w); Erickson et al. 2012, PLoS ONE (doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0031781); Chin et al. 1998, Nature (doi:10.1038/31461).

scenes.narration: One T. rex bite pressed down like three small cars stacked on its teeth.
Scientists rebuilt its jaw muscles from its closest living relatives, crocodiles and birds.
Their estimate: up to thirty-four thousand five hundred newtons at the back teeth. More than twice the strongest bite ever measured, a saltwater crocodile's.
Its pointed teeth focused all that force onto tiny tips, hard enough to shatter bone.
We know it did. A giant fossil poop, likely from a T. rex, is up to half crushed bone.
So why would a giant hunter bother eating the bones?
